lab_title: VSEPR: From Lewis Structure to 3D Molecular Geometry (AR Lab)
top_level_objectives: Apply VSEPR theory to predict electron-domain and molecular geometries from a Lewis structure.
Differentiate electron-domain geometries (linear through octahedral) from molecular geometries (including lone-pair effects).
Use AR representations to identify lone pairs vs bonding pairs and determine expected bond angles and deviations.
Compare VSEPR predictions with real molecular examples (H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, XeF4) and explain discrepancies via lone-pair repulsions and lone-pair steric effects.

scenes.brief_purpose: Connect the 2D Lewis structure to the 3D “electron-domain” concept that VSEPR uses.
key_visuals: A floating 2D Lewis structure of a sample molecule with the central atom highlighted
Animated markers that convert each lone pair and bond pair into labeled “electron domains” radiating from the central atom
A simple repulsion-energy meter that will later change as domains move
student_actions: Identify the central atom and count total electron domains (bonding pairs + lone pairs)
Classify the electron domains as either “lone pair” or “bonding pair” using the on-screen legend
Predict the electron-domain geometry category before any AR rearrangement (e.g., linear/trigonal planar/etc.)

scenes.scene_name: Scene 2: Electron-Domain Geometries as Repulsion-Minimizing Arrangements
scenes.brief_purpose: Build the mental model that each electron-domain geometry is the lowest-repulsion arrangement.
key_visuals: Five “target” layouts shown as an interactive set: linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral
A repulsion map (e.g., colored arrows or intensity bands) around the central atom
A toggle to switch between 2D plan view and 3D spatial view
student_actions: Match the electron-domain count from the previous scene to one of the five target geometries
Rotate the model to confirm relative angles between domains (e.g., 180°, 120°, 109.5°, 90°/120°, 180°/90°)
State the ideal bond-angle expectations associated with that electron-domain geometry (without yet applying lone-pair modifications)

scenes.scene_name: Scene 3: Lone Pairs as Geometry Modifiers (Electron vs Molecular Geometry)
scenes.brief_purpose: Teach how lone pairs compress the arrangement of bonding pairs, producing molecular geometries that differ from electron-domain geometries.
key_visuals: A split-screen: electron-domain skeleton vs molecular-shape “boundary” that only shows atoms/bonding directions
Selectable lone pairs that increase repulsion influence compared to bonding pairs (e.g., stronger repulsion coloring)
A slider or step button labeled “Minimize Repulsion” that gradually settles the model
student_actions: Designate which electron domains are lone pairs and observe how they push bonding domains closer
Compare the electron-domain geometry to the resulting molecular geometry label (e.g., tetrahedral electron domain → bent/trigonal pyramidal)
Record the expected directional change as a qualitative bond-angle trend (smaller vs larger than ideal)

scenes.scene_name: Scene 4: Guided Case Studies—Bent → Trigonal Pyramidal → Seesaw
scenes.brief_purpose: Apply VSEPR to specific common molecular shapes within the first three electron-domain families.
key_visuals: Three interactive molecule cards that animate from ideal electron-domain scaffolds to lone-pair-modified molecular shapes
Case sequence visuals: bent (e.g., H2O), trigonal pyramidal (e.g., NH3), seesaw (e.g., SF4—optional visualization)
Real-time bond-angle readouts showing ideal vs predicted angles with a “deviation” indicator
student_actions: For each case card, place or confirm lone pairs and bonding positions around the central atom
Use the AR model to choose the correct molecular geometry label (bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw)
Explain, in one sentence, whether the bond angle should be smaller than the ideal and why (lone pairs occupy more space)

scenes.scene_name: Scene 5: Five and Six Electron Domains—T-shaped, Square Planar, Square Pyramidal
scenes.brief_purpose: Extend VSEPR from trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral electron domains to the remaining common molecular shapes.
key_visuals: Animated trigonal bipyramidal scaffold with axial vs equatorial sites labeled
Animated octahedral scaffold with visible missing-ligand cases to form square planar and square pyramidal
A comparison overlay showing lone-pair vs bond-pair repulsion leading to axial/equatorial preferences (when relevant)
student_actions: Choose locations for lone pairs/bonding pairs on axial/equatorial or octahedral sites to minimize repulsion
Identify molecular geometries produced after accounting for lone pairs (T-shaped, square planar, square pyramidal)
Predict whether any observed angles deviate more when lone pairs are in axial vs equatorial-like positions (qualitative reasoning)

scenes.scene_name: Scene 6: Real Molecule Matching and Bond-Angle Deviations
scenes.brief_purpose: Validate predictions by comparing to known molecular structures and explain deviations from ideal VSEPR angles.
key_visuals: Side-by-side panels for: water, ammonia, methane, PF5, SF6, XeF4
For each, an AR model with predicted geometry overlay and an observed-structure marker
Bond-angle readouts highlighting the classic comparison: H2O (~104.5°) vs CH4 (109.5°) and other measured trends
student_actions: Match each real molecule to the correct electron-domain and molecular geometry predictions
For at least two molecules, compute/describe the bond-angle deviation from the ideal value
State the explanation for deviations in terms of relative repulsion: lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs
